title: Nuclear radiation and conservation in decay
prior_knowledge_summary: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons and is very small compared with the atom.
Proton number Z fixes element identity, nucleon number A counts protons and neutrons, and a nuclide is written as ^A_Z X.
Isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
new_learning: Compare the composition, approximate mass and charge of alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma radiation.
Use conservation of nucleon number and charge to complete alpha and beta nuclear decay equations.

learning_outcomes.text: Understand that nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
Describe the composition, mass and charge of alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma radiations.
Represent alpha and beta decay using radioactive decay equations.

blocks.heading: How can a nucleus change its name without losing track of anything?
content: A uranium nucleus emits a tiny object and becomes thorium. The element has changed, yet the nuclear numbers still balance exactly.
The puzzle has two parts. We must identify what left the nucleus, then keep separate accounts for nucleon number and charge.

figure.purpose: Create the conservation puzzle before naming the emitted radiation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of one large labelled parent nucleus, an arrow, a smaller daughter nucleus and an unidentified emitted cluster shown as a question mark. Put two blank balance ledgers below for nucleon number and charge. Do not reveal the particle identity or completed numbers.
figure.alt_text: A parent nucleus changes into a daughter nucleus while an unidentified particle is emitted.

blocks.heading: Four radiations carry different cargo
content: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons. It has nucleon number 4, charge +2e and mass about 4 u.

A beta-minus particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus. It has nucleon number 0, charge -e and a mass that is very small compared with 1 u. A beta-plus particle is a positron emitted from the nucleus. It also has nucleon number 0 and very small mass, but charge +e.
Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation. It has no nucleons, zero charge and zero rest mass. These identities, not how fast a radiation happens to move, decide how it enters a nuclear equation.

figure.purpose: Compare composition, mass and charge without relying on prose memory.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table with columns alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma and rows composition, nucleon number, approximate mass and charge. Use small particle sketches and a restrained colour key. Keep later neutrino and antiparticle language absent.
figure.alt_text: A comparison table shows the composition, nucleon number, approximate mass and charge of four nuclear radiations.

blocks.heading: A field can reveal charge
content: Imagine the four radiations crossing the same electric field. Alpha bends toward the negative plate because it is positive. Beta-minus bends toward the positive plate because it is negative. Beta-plus bends toward the negative plate because it is positive. Gamma is not deflected because it is uncharged.

Beta particles curve more strongly than alpha particles in the same conditions because their masses are far smaller. Direction diagnoses the sign of charge; the amount of bending also depends on mass and motion.

A common idea is that gamma must be neutral because it travels straight. That reasoning is incomplete: a charged particle can also travel straight when no transverse field acts. Gamma stays undeflected in a transverse electric field because its charge is zero.

figure.purpose: Connect charge sign and relative mass to field deflection.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper path sketch between horizontal charged plates. Show alpha and beta-plus curving toward the negative plate, beta-minus toward the positive plate, and gamma straight. Make beta curves visibly stronger than alpha. Use short labels only.
figure.alt_text: Charged nuclear radiations bend in opposite directions in an electric field while gamma travels straight.

blocks.heading: Two ledgers must balance
content: In every nuclear process, total nucleon number before equals total nucleon number after. Total charge before also equals total charge after. In nuclide notation these are the upper and lower numbers, so balance the two rows separately.

For alpha decay, the emitted alpha particle is ^4_2He. The daughter therefore has A reduced by 4 and Z reduced by 2. For beta-minus emission, the emitted particle is ^0_-1e. The daughter keeps the same A and has Z increased by 1 so that its charge plus -1 still matches the parent.

For beta-plus emission, the emitted particle is ^0_+1e. The daughter keeps the same A and has Z decreased by 1. This lesson uses only the bookkeeping visible in these equations; the additional particles involved in beta decay come next.

figure.purpose: Make the separate A and Z conservation ledgers visible.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper double-ledger diagram. One row balances upper numbers A and one row balances lower charge numbers Z. Include generic alpha, beta-minus and beta-plus templates with daughter entries blank. Do not include neutrinos.
figure.alt_text: Separate ledgers balance nucleon number and charge number in three types of nuclear decay.

blocks.heading: Walk through an alpha decay
content: Start with ^{226}_{88}Ra and alpha emission. Write ^{226}_{88}Ra -> daughter + ^4_2He. For nucleon number, 226 = A + 4, so A = 222. For charge, 88 = Z + 2, so Z = 86.
Proton number 86 identifies radon, so the completed equation is ^{226}_{88}Ra -> ^{222}_{86}Rn + ^4_2He.
Check independently by adding the products: 222 + 4 = 226 and 86 + 2 = 88. Both ledgers balance, and the daughter element agrees with Z = 86.

figure.purpose: Model a complete alpha-decay method with an independent check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout for radium-226 alpha decay. Use four boxes: write emitted particle, solve A, solve Z, identify daughter. Finish with two addition checks in a contrasting colour.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout balances nucleon and charge numbers to complete radium-226 alpha decay.

blocks.heading: Beta decay changes Z but not A
content: For beta-minus emission from ^{32}_{15}P, write ^{32}_{15}P -> daughter + ^0_-1e. Nucleon number gives 32 = A + 0, so A = 32. Charge gives 15 = Z - 1, so Z = 16. The daughter is sulfur: ^{32}_{15}P -> ^{32}_{16}S + ^0_-1e.
For beta-plus emission from ^{22}_{11}Na, nucleon number remains 22. Charge gives 11 = Z + 1, so Z = 10. The daughter is neon: ^{22}_{11}Na -> ^{22}_{10}Ne + ^0_+1e.

It can feel as if emitting a negative beta particle should make the daughter less positive. The equation shows why that fails: the daughter charge must rise by one so that daughter charge plus the emitted -1 still equals the parent charge.

figure.purpose: Contrast the opposite Z changes in beta-minus and beta-plus decay.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split worked board. Left: phosphorus-32 beta-minus with A unchanged and Z moving 15 to 16. Right: sodium-22 beta-plus with A unchanged and Z moving 11 to 10. Include the charge sums 16 + (-1) = 15 and 10 + 1 = 11.
figure.alt_text: Parallel beta-minus and beta-plus examples show unchanged nucleon number and opposite changes in proton number.

blocks.heading: Identify, balance, then check
content: Use one reliable route. First identify the emitted radiation and write its upper and lower numbers. Next balance A. Then balance charge number Z. Use the resulting Z to identify the daughter element, and finally add both product rows as a check.

Alpha carries four nucleons and +2e. Beta-minus and beta-plus carry no nucleons and charges -e and +e. Gamma carries no nucleons and no charge. Therefore alpha changes A and Z, beta changes only Z, and gamma emission changes neither A nor Z.
This conservation model is enough for radiation identities and decay equations. Why beta decay also involves another particle, and why beta energies form a range, belongs to the next lesson.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact decision route without solving later practice items.

figure.alt_text: A decision flow and change table summarize how to complete and check nuclear decay equations.

misconceptions_addressed: Gamma is known to be neutral merely because it can travel straight.
Emitting a negative beta particle must make the daughter proton number smaller.
next_lesson_can_assume: Alpha is a helium nucleus with A = 4 and charge +2e.
Beta-minus and beta-plus have A = 0 and charges -e and +e respectively.
Gamma has A = 0 and zero charge.
Nucleon number and charge can be balanced to complete alpha and beta decay equations.
